name: Kumbainggar
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kumbainggar/Gumbaynggir is not in the catalog (no-catalog-record). The single sweep item, Kager 1995 'On foot templates and root templates', is open access on the Benjamins platform; fetched sources, saved and read (section 5, pp. 133-135). It is about Gumbaynggir word stress but wholly second-hand from Eades 1979: stress on the heavy (long-vowel) syllable, otherwise initial with optional second-syllable stress in 3+ syllable words; foot analysed as uneven iamb [H]/[LH]/[LL]; length (and stress) shifts to syllable 2 when HL nouns take case suffixes. The first-hand statement of record remains Eades 1979 p. 268 (section 2.3), already on file from a prior lane and re-read from the page image this sweep: stress on a long vowel > else on a vowel+semivowel syllable > else initial, with optional medial stress in longer words; Kager's summary omits the vowel+semivowel clause. Prior lane's records Smythe 1948-50 (Oceania, Wiley-paywalled) and Morelli 2008 (Muurrbay, print-only) as unfetched; Kager fetch and md5sums appended to Nothing left to acquire for this item; if the language is ever coded, Eades 1979 p. 268 is the deciding source with Kager 1995 as a supporting analysis.

new_statements.quote: In Gumbaynggir words, the stress falls on [1] a long vowel [2] (or if there is no long vowel) a syllable-final vowel plus semivowel cluster. (If there are two such sequences in a word, stress occurs on the first.) [3] (or if neither of the above applies) on the first vowel, with the exception that in a word of three or more syllables one of the middle vowels may receive stress. [...] However there is a strong tendency for the initial vowel to be deleted and the second syllable stressed in a word with the initial syllable either /Cuw/ or /Ciy/: /buwa:r/ [bwá:r] 'baby'; /giyaŋari/ [gyéŋari] 'schnapper'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive: primary stress goes to the syllable with a long vowel; failing that, to the first syllable closed by a vowel+semivowel (diphthong-like) sequence; failing both, to the first syllable. Since heavy syllables occur only in the first two syllables (Goedemans 1998 on Eades' data), this amounts to initial stress unless the second syllable is heavy (mí:mi, ŋámi, gáwgan vs ŋalí:, ŋalú:ŋgir, gamáy).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Eades. Goedemans 1998 (secondary) infers no final secondary stress from ŋáliwan.
new_statements.exceptions: In words of three or more syllables one of the middle vowels may receive stress (gálugun ~ galúgun 'one'); words beginning /Cuw/ or /Ciy/ tend to lose the initial vowel and stress the second syllable ([bwá:r], [gyéŋari]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('In Gumbaynggir words'); examples are citation forms; phrase intonation discussed separately for interrogatives (rising intonation on the last word).
new_statements.identity_note: Eades 1979 describes Gumbaynggir (= Gumbaynggirr, ISO kgs, glottocode kumb1268) as a whole, drawing on 1970s speakers of the Nambucca-Bellinger region and Smythe's earlier data; she notes northern vs southern variation (§1) but the stress statement is not dialect-specific. Glottolog names the language Kumbainggar; the earlier scan verdict SOURCE-NAMED-UNREACHABLE is superseded because the ANU Open Research scan of Handbook of Australian Languages vol. 1 (hdl:1885/114846) is open and was already on file.

new_statements.citation: Eades, Diana (1979). Gumbaynggir. In R.M.W. Dixon & Barry J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, vol. 1, 244-361. Amsterdam: John Benjamins / Canberra: ANU Press. Section 2.3 Stress, p. 268.
new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive, non-fixed stress with initial default: stress goes to the (first) long vowel; failing that to a syllable closed by a semivowel (Vy/Vw); failing that to the first syllable, with optional shift to a medial syllable in words of three or more syllables (galugun ~ galúgun). Since long vowels are confined to the first two syllables (Kager 1995's census of Eades' vocabulary, and Eades' own length-shift rule in 2.4), main stress always lands on syllable 1 or 2. First-hand descriptive source (Eades' own fieldwork), and the source every later treatment (Kager 1995, Goedemans 1998) cites.

sources.quote: In Gumbaynggir words, the stress falls on [1] a long vowel [2] (or if there is no long vowel) a syllable-final vowel plus semivowel cluster. (If there are two such sequences in a word, stress occurs on the first.) [3] (or if neither of the above applies) on the first vowel, with the exception that in a word of three or more syllables one of the middle vowels may receive stress. [...] However there is a strong tendency for the initial vowel to be deleted and the second syllable stressed in a word with the initial syllable either /Cuw/ or /Ciy/: /buwa:r/ [bwá:r] 'baby'; /giyaŋari/ [gyéŋari] 'schnapper'.
sources.note: Section 2.3 Stress (p. 268): stress falls on a long vowel; else on the first syllable-final vowel+semivowel sequence; else on the first vowel, with the exception that in words of 3+ syllables a middle vowel may be stressed; initial /Cuw/ /Ciy/ syllables tend to lose their vowel with stress shifting to the second syllable. No mention of secondary stress. Examples mí:mi 'mother', ŋámi 'woman', ŋalí: '1du inc', ŋalú:ŋgir 'clever man', gamáy 'spear', ŋáliwan 'jewfish', gáwgan 'shield', gálugun~galúgun 'one', má:nay 'take-PRES'.

sources.note: Second-hand, citing Eades 1979: 'Main stress in Gumbaynggirr is on the first syllable unless the second syllable is heavy. Heavy syllables are those with a long vowel or a vowel - semi-vowel sequence'; heavy syllables occur only in the first two syllables; no final secondary stress in áliwan; QS trochees, left-to-right, degenerate feet forbidden.

sources.citation: Kager, René (1995). On foot templates and root templates. Linguistics in the Netherlands 12(1): 125-138. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (AVT Publications).
sources.quote: Let us first look into the stress pattern. Stress falls on a heavy syllable (17a-d). When there are no heavy syllables, stress is initial and optionally on the second syllable of words longer than two syllables (17e-f): (17) a [ŋuum] 'smoke' b [mii].mi 'mother' c [ŋa.lii] '1du inc S,A' d [ŋa.luuŋ].gir 'clever man' e [ŋá.mi] 'woman' f [ga.lu].gun or [ga.lu].gun 'one'. That is, the stress foot is minimally bimoraic and maximally disyllabic, with vowel length aligning with right edge of foot: the 'uneven iamb' [H], [LH], [LL]. [...] default prominence in [LL] feet is trochaic, but lapse avoidance in trisyllabic words causes optional second syllable stress
sources.locator: Section 5 'Gumbaynggir', pp. 133-134, root census (16) and stress summary (17); length shift under suffixation (20), pp. 134-135
sources.note: Second-hand theoretical treatment built entirely on Eades 1979 (a census of 473 roots from her vocabulary). Stress falls on the heavy (long-vowel) syllable; otherwise initial, with optional second-syllable stress in words of more than two syllables. Kager notes that vowel length never occurs outside the first two root syllables and that no two adjacent heavy syllables occur, so main stress is always within the first two syllables; he analyses the foot as an uneven iamb [H]/[LH]/[LL] with default trochaic prominence in [LL]. Also documents obligatory length shift from first to second syllable…
